utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to briefly address a few matters. First of all, the Chamber would very much like to conclude the testimony of this witness today. If we would not manage to do that before quarter to 2.00, then there are a few options. Either to extend slightly the last session in the morning. If that would not be sufficient, we would consider to additionally sit this afternoon. Unfortunately, it's not possible to do that at the beginning of the afternoon because there would not even be two Judges. Therefore, we would then re-start later this afternoon. But, to the extent possible, the Chamber would urge the parties to see whether they with conduct their cross-examinations in such a way that we could conclude in the normal sessions. That is one. Second. Mr. Jordash, we received yesterday a message about the availability of Sir Ivor Roberts. This Chamber has accommodated in every respect all the wishes. We have scheduled him exactly on the day -- even after we had to wait a month, we scheduled him exactly on the day you indicated he was available. Now if would be a matter of one or two days, then we might even then consider - I'm not saying that we will - we would consider to change that date slightly. But now another two months is really not something that the Chamber can accept. And if you say he can't make it, to testify in a court is a civil duty, and the Stanisic Defence knows exactly that if a witness prioritises his activities in such a way that he would be unavailable for giving testimony, that, of course, you, as the calling party, you know exactly how to obtain the support of the Chamber to -- to -- let me say to encourage the witness to appear in court at such a time that it still makes sense to hear his testimony. You know exactly how to do that. I'm not going to further expand on that. Of course, the preferable way would be to come to an agreement one way or another. But we even on the days he would arrive then, he should return then, we fully accommodated that after having waited for month. So, therefore, there is not an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hear what you're saying precisely, and we've appreciated - and we do appreciate - how patient Your Honour has been with this issue, and we're going to do everything we can to ensure that the Court and this trial is -- is not in any way obstructed by this particular witness. And we apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You do not have to apologise. Well, it's apparently -- I -- I -- the Chamber doesn't think that it's the Stanisic Defence which is to be blamed in any way for it, and the Defence, as always, has the full support of the Chamber to present its witnesses as it deems fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were the matters I'd like to raise. Good morning, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the office has announced to me as I arrived here that I would be testifying roughly for eight hours, and this covered both the Prosecution and the Defence. The yesterday's hearing was highly stressful for me, not because of you, but because of certain obligations that await me as I return home. Let me tell you that as a result of my work for the mission that -- on which suspicions have been cast here, I had to undergo a heart surgery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Mr., Mr. -- No suspicion has been cast on anything. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly request that should I feel ill - this is nitroglycerin - may I be allowed to sit aside or leave the courtroom in order to inject myself with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need in that respect, please address me, and then we'll consider your request. And, of course, we would always allow you to take whatever necessary measure in order to not to suffer any physical damage. So that would mean that we would allow you to leave the court for that. Then, of course, we would inquire in how much time that takes, et cetera. But please be assured that should you address me, that we'll take the appropriate approach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two minutes more, please. Over the first break, I will receive the medical findings concerning my blood pressure, which is decisive for my future treatment. Secondly, Your Honours, I would kindly ask you to instruct the Defence to insert into the file of the documents that I brought along and gave to them this thank you note from the Croatian authorities where they address me as the chief of police and express their gratitude. This may be of significance for my further discussions with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are free to submit what they want to submit, and to make it a condition for future conversations with the Prosecution is not something this Chamber would expect you to do. But the Chamber is not ordering any party to do any such thing. I also say this, now knowing approximately what the document is about, parties are free to do it. If they wish not to do it, the Chamber will not order them. Please be seated, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And you may have noticed already that the Chamber tries to do its utmost best to have your examination be concluded today so that you can leave The Hague after that. Ms. Marcus, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I please have private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, when we stopped yesterday, I was asking you about certain individuals in relation to Bosanski Samac. Please answer as briefly as possible. I'll just give you a name. You can just tell me what their position was, to your knowledge, in Bosanski Samac. Do you know Milan Josic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Active-duty captain of the Yugoslav People's Army, with the air force. His position was that of commander of the Obudovac Special Detachment; one of the elite units. He was later to become the Chief of Staff of the Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Milan Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An intelligence officer with the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Jovan Kujundzic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the family name of Kujundzic. Or I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sasa Culibrk.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Nenad Mitic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Davor Subotic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And, finally, for this list, Aleksandar Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there's been evidence --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- in this case that prior to the takeover of Bosanski Samac, and prior to the arrival by helicopter of the volunteers at Batkusa, to which you testified, the SDS Main Board suggested to the commander of Tactical Group 17, Stevan Nikolic, that they recruit through friends and acquaintances of the SDS members in Samac in the Serbian MUP, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, and Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli, and a group of 30 men from the FRY to assist in the takeover of Bosanski Samac. Now although you testified that you did not enjoy credibility with the SDS, were you aware of this suggestion made to Stevan Nikolic? Kindly, a yes or no answer will suffice, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There's also been evidence that members of the SRS were sent along with Crni and Debeli as part of this training. Isn't that accurate, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is accurate that they were sent along, but I am not aware of Crni and Debeli being involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer you to P1516 and P1417.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: According to the evidence in this case, approximately 18 volunteers from Samac were added to this group from the FRY, plus Crni and Debeli, and all 50 or so of them were trained in Lezimir and then in Ilok. You were not involved in any way in the training in Lezimir or Pajzos prior to the take-over of Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did indicate that it was only the JNA that I recognised; whereas, the other structures, specifically the paramilitaries, were not of interest to me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus you referred to first to Lezimir and then Ilok and then later Lezimir or Pajzos. Is there any risk that the witness would be confused by that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first time I mentioned I had said Ilok, Pajzos. Perhaps it's not reflected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You knew that I when I said Ilok, I was talking about Pajzos. Did you understand that in my question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You made a couple of mistakes but I don't have the right to correct you. Batkusa was mispronounced, and it's not the Main Board of the SDS but the municipal board. But I was cautioned to give a yes or no answer, so I will adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Matters are sufficiently clear, I think. Please proceed. Oh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, may we have a reference for the last question, please, the evidence that my learned friend is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to give it. It's P1576 and P1416. P1576 and P1416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you were asked earlier in your testimony about Pajzos, you answered: "It was a listening centre, and I was not responsible for that centre, nor was I well versed in what was going on there. I did not have access to it." I believe your comment referred to the pre-war period. Did you have occasion to visit Pajzos any time in 1991 or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mentioned on several occasions. I arrived in the area on 15th of March, 1993, and the laws of physics that dictate that I could not have been in two places at once. Let me explain to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned Pajzos, but we didn't catch what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I interrupted you, I'm sorry. I'm just trying to focus. Before the takeover of Bosanski Samac, did you have occasion to visit Pajzos between 1991 and up until the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 1991 and 1993, I was not present in the area of Vukovar at all. It was an area where fighting was going on, and I -- I wasn't able to access the area at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: There's been evidence presented in this case that Franko Simatovic came to the training ground at Ilok, Pajzos, held a briefing, and informed those who had been trained that they were to be deployed to Bosanski Samac by helicopter and that the objective was to secure Bosanski Samac and the surrounding villages. In attendance at this briefing, according to the evidence, were Debeli, Crni, and Stevan Todorovic. Were you ever informed of this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P1516.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know the name of Franko Simatovic. Let me just say that I didn't need any volunteers or anyone else to train special police units because I know that myself very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you were not aware of the role of Franko Simatovic in training, planning, or ordering in connection to the Bosanski Samac takeover; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I heard of Simatovic only from people lacking in seriousness, braggarts who thought that they would add to their own significance if they said that they were in his company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your testimony at page 17942, you described the arrival of Stevan Todorovic and a number of volunteers by helicopter to Batkusa - I hope I pronounced it correct this time. According to the evidence in this case, this deployment to Bosanski Samac occurred the day after the briefing by Franko Simatovic. This group arrived in Bosanski Samac the day before you were invited to the meeting to advise the public security station; is that correct? Yes or no, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question is very complex. There is the role of Simatovic that the witness knows nothing about, the arrival of the helicopters at Batkusa, the meeting that the witness attended. So what -- what, in fact, is witness being asked? What kind of answer is he supposed to give to this? There are at least four or five questions contained in this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I considered only the last line to be the question. Is it correct that the group that arrived, that they arrived the day before you were invited for the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I cannot answer with a simple "yes" or "no" when Madam Prosecutor keeps using the term that I was a councillor of the public security station which is not feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is why the question has been rephrased. And Ms. Marcus will take care that questions will not necessarily be composite and clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you stated that these volunteers agreed to be under the command of the 17th Tactical Group. In fact, other evidence in this cases conforms with that information that you provided. According to this evidence, two days before the takeover, Dragan Djordjevic, aka, Crni, had attended a meeting with Todorovic, Blagoje Simic, and others. And they discussed, including the Red Berets, in the existing 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P1576.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, here's my question to you. As soon as combat operations began, Crni and his group were, in fact, temporarily subordinated to TG 17 which was comprised of a combination of those from the FRY and the volunteers from Samac who had been trained in Pajzos and Lezimir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite correct. However, I would like to note that among the group that arrived in Batkusa, there was also a group of local men who had worked in Serbia or Croatia earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I refer Your Honours to P1416, in connection with that previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you then described the takeover of the public security station on the night of the 16th to 17th of April, 1992. You said, though, that Colonel Nikolic, commander of the 17th Tactical Group, was "not kept abreast of these things." So Nikolic did not lead the takeover of the public security station on the night of the 16th to 17th April, 1992. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's not a takeover but, rather, a restructuring of this station because half of the Serbs were already in the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So it was rather the volunteers who arrived with Stevan Todorovic who led that restructuring of the station, as you say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, he offered to some Croats and Muslims to continue working there, but under rules that he would enforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow, the interpretation that the witness received was not clear enough. It wasn't clear whether what was referred to was Stevan Todorovic, the volunteers, or all of them. So the interpretation was not clear enough for the witness to answer properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness answered the question. But perhaps you'd verify whether he understood the question well, Ms. Marcus. And perhaps by -- in view of the answer he gave, to seek confirmation that he understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic I will repeat my question and your answer to you. My question was: "So it was rather the volunteers who arrived with Stevan Todorovic who led that restructuring of the station, as you say?" Your answer was: "Yes. However, he offered to some Croats and Muslims to continue working there, but under rules that he would enforce." Did you understand my question and is that the appropriate answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand it, and I'm very pleased with the way you are questioning me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you testified that Simo Zaric complained to Stevan Nikolic about these volunteers who had arrived by helicopter and that Nikolic replied: "That the Government of Serbia, in a decree of 1992, proclaimed that volunteers could report to fight." So is it your evidence that the volunteers who arrived were those who were authorised by the government of Serbia to come volunteer to join the fight in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did I say that, nor was it that way. The government allows its citizens to volunteer, especially if they hail from a certain area, and it certainly would not send anyone to another area. That's not the government's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, my question was whether the volunteers were authorised by the government of Serbia to come volunteer. Your answer says that the government allows its citizens to volunteer. Can you tell us -- can you tell us which branch of the government of Serbia you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to a -- to an act, actually, of -- a legal act, and that law is actually implemented by other organs or other departments. If you allow me, a provision in Serbia -- or, rather, a decree in Serbia is a sub-law or a bylaw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Djukic, what Ms. Marcus would like to know is what authority would approve volunteers to -- to join in military activity. Under that law and bylaws.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm in Serbia and I will not be punished if I go to the battle-field in Bosanski Samac. But the state does not have any obligation in respect of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that the decree that proclaimed that volunteers could report to fight, that all volunteers - without any further decision - would be free once they had reported themselves to join in such military activity, or was there any decision needed to approve the joinder of volunteers in the military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone had to subordinate themselves to the Yugoslav People's Army. That was the obligation. But in Belgrade, a large number of centres sprang up that actually organised volunteers and the first person who did that - and he was never taken to account for that - was Vuk Draskovic and his guard went to Gospic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You testified at page 17954 that you went to speak to Debeli after Nikolic left the area to ask him for reinforcements. Do you recall the date of this discussion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early June. But I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What kind of reinforcements were you talking about? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had exclusively to do with the intervention platoon in Pelagicevo. I was trained and I took part in the training, and this involved exclusively people from Pelagici; acquaintances or even friends, I could say, of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What position was Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli, in, that you asked him to provide reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then-Chief of Staff of the Posavina Brigade, who was the chief operative in the brigade, and subordinated to Commander Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When asked about your conversation with Debeli, you said at page 17955: "He said that they had to fight really hard to appoint those duties," I believe you meant "to be appointed to those duties," "that is correct. They were the first people, members of the brigade who had not graduated from the Military Academy of the Yugoslavia army. He told me that it was a great pity that I was on the wrong side, that I was not a member of the SDS, and only after I explained to him what I was and that I had passed with my units without any losses, he told me that he had been a police non-commissioned officer, that he was dismissed from the police, that he had a very negative view of us, people who still supported Tito's idealogy, Milosevic's ideology, and that of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. He asked me -- and he asked me, once again, to try and change my position. And he even said that if I were to join this radical party, that I might even be conferred a rank there." Weren't you already part of the JNA with a rank?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He considered that I was a promising individual because I was 48 years old, and he thought that I could become a Chetnik Vojvoda, duke. Except that instead of the SDS, it should be the Radical Party, where you read the SDS there. Or perhaps it was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now your evidence is that when you spoke to Debeli he did not mention that he was Serbian DB. Is that how you knew that Debeli was not affiliated with the Serbian DB? Is that how you drew that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In brief, I was equally well acquainted with public and state security, which you can also see if you read one of my studies. Now, the security of Serbia had, under its operative control, both Vojvoda Seselj and all his men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you explain what you meant by "I was equally well acquainted with public and state security"? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- a well-educated member of the police, the only general from that period who is still alive and free.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now you said, according to the transcript, the state -- "the security of Serbia had, under its operative control, both Vojvoda Seselj and all his men." Are you saying that the State Security Service of Serbia had Seselj under their control? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. At one point in time, he was even in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now to go back to my original question -- I'm sorry. One moment, please. Sorry, Mr. Djukic, just in response -- my last question was about Seselj. And you said: "Certainly. At one point in time, he was even in prison." What -- what time are you talking about; and for what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For unauthorised trips to Kosovo where he fermented -- where he fermented unrest among the Albanians. So he was sentenced to a prison term of a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, I'm really trying to understand exactly what you are saying, so pardon me repeated questions on this. Are you saying that Seselj was being -- was under the control of the state security; or are you saying they were monitoring his activities, operatively speaking? What precisely are you saying about the relationship between the Serbian state security and Seselj?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surveillance. Now, in what manner and how frequently, I don't know because that was something that was considered secret of that service, and I was not a member of the service, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now going back to the question about Debeli. You told us that you believed that he was not affiliated with the Serbian SDB. Was that based on the fact that he didn't mention that he was so affiliated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I presided over an inter-republic commission for the promotion and improvement of work of the service, and I said that if you were once dismissed from a service, if a staff member was once in -- once dismissed from a service, that he would never again be able to apply and to be employed by any other service in the former Yugoslavia. And, as for him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your question [sic] where you said, "And as for him," apparently referring to Debeli. What did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was sacked. He was dismissed from the Public Security Service of Serbia. And such a person would never again be employable anywhere in Yugoslavia as an active policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake when I put "question," but that's clear on the transcript now. Of course, I was referring to the answer of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So that is your assumption. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that was the conclusion. That was a conclusion, an obligation. If a person was dismissed from service in Kragujevac, he would not be employable in Osijek, for instance. That was our joint position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you also testified at page 17954 that you had an occasion to speak with Crni directly. In fact, you later told us that you spoke to him more thereafter, but this was the first time you mentioned that. And this was when you went to ask for his assistance. Do you recall when this was? Was this just at the time in June 1992, after you spoke with Debeli?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was very important to me to protect my village because all my property had been seized in Zagreb, and other than human lives, the property that I owned was at -- was valuable. It was some 400.000 German marks. That would be what I would assess it as. And you agree that would be even a lot for this country, let alone for my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You also testified that quote -- that you, "... addressed him as a proper soldier. And he told me, You are in no way bound to stand before me as a soldier would." So did Crni not view you as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But from some sources in Pelagicevo, he learned about my credibility and my biography. And unlike some people there, he knew that I was much better versed than he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You said: "Crni said that he had some information about me and that he was more than glad to accept me as his corroborator and that I was yet to benefit from my acquaintance with him." How would Crni have had this information about you? Is it what you just said, from some sources in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the SDS, Dusan Tanasic and Crni knew that the citizens of Pelagicevo were in favour of my taking over the brigade and not him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who appointed Crni as commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily he was appointed by the SDS, but the then-acting Drincic [phoen] or Dencic who was a colonel at the Drina Corps, he was the one who issued this order at the insistence of the SDS because Crni was the first civilian who headed the army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness did not fully complete his sentence. Could he please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps reference is incorrect, and I see that the interpreters also had a remark to make, that not everything was reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat the last part of your answer? You told us that he was the one who issued this order at the insistence of the SDS because Crni was the first civilian who headed the army. And what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That Dencic was an acting -- of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, which is the largest military formation in the area of Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P1417.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, what I'm going to show you now on your screen is a statement made by Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I please have page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I please have page 3 in English and also page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the paragraph starting: "At the beginning of April..." It says: "At the beginning of April, a group of Radical Party members went to training at the training centre near Ilok in the town of Pajzos. A group of 18 men from Samac also came to the centre for training. I was at the centre as an instructor, although I attended to other jobs and did not train these specific men. When they concluded their training, these men returned to Samac, and 30 men from Serbia went with them as reinforcement. I was with these volunteers, as was Aleksandar Vukovic, who was killed, and we headed for Samac as volunteers. We went for patriotic reasons to help the Serbian people in the fight." As can you see, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, himself describes his involvement in the preparatory training for the takeover of Bosanski Samac. I'll point you to another part of this document and then ask you a few questions. At the next paragraph it says: "The entire group arrived by helicopter at the village of Batkusa on 11 April 1992. Following a decision of the Samac authorities and with the approval of Lieutenant-Colonel Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, the entire group was attached to the army, and on 17 April 1992, between 50 and 60 of us entered Samac under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. This unit was composed of Radical Party members from Serbia, people from Samac who were at the training centre, and some others who were attached. After the liberation of Samac and the clearing of the surrounding villages, there is confirmation for the establishment of a special purposes battalion. This is what the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Stevan Nikolic, requested and issued an order with a view to this. I was appointed commander of the battalion, and after its establishment, this battalion went to break through a corridor towards Brcko." This report by Crni is in conformity with the evidence you have given; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, save for the fact that Crni did not break the corridor open to Brcko. It was a minor-scale blockade in a village. Captain Brkic with an armoured mechanized unit who broke the corridor open.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend spent reading to the witness half a page worth of text on something that he had already spoken to only to ask him if this was correct. And there's at least ten facts contained in that segment, in that portion, where he is supposed to answer whether it's correct or not, and he had already spoken to certain issues and presented views that differed from those contained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is your objection, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the questions are -- confused the witness and they are designed to be misleading rather than to shed light for Their Honours' benefit. Each and every part or fact contained there should be put to the witness and asked to get his confirmation on if it's correct or not, rather than to putting a question that would relate to all these facts together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Ms. Marcus did is she put a piece of evidence before the witness to give him an opportunity to comment on it or to state that it is in conformity with his own evidence, and that's exactly what the witness did. He said this is all conform my testimony, apart from one point, and then he referred to something which is not in the statement - that is that the breakthrough to Brcko, because the part read to him was only about whether they went to do that, not that they did yet. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission. I'm sorry to interrupt. Five minutes ago the witness said that he knew nothing --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Please forgive me. If Mr. Petrovic would like to put different aspects of this to the witness on re-examination, he's perfectly entitled to do so. But to go back now and basically do a re-examination in the middle of the cross-examination, Your Honours, I feel is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And certainly not in the form that you start discussing the evidence. If you have any further questions for the witness, you can put them in re-examination, Mr. Petrovic, and you are fully entitled to challenge whatever the witness said in cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, was arrested, and he spent about ten days in detention according to the evidence in this case. Were you informed of Crni's arrest?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I had no part in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, that reference was to P1417 and P1416.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know why Crni was arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of wilful behaviour and the attempt to break the corridor open at Crkvine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I have please P1416, page 3 in English and page 4 in B/C/S. P1416.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see coming up on the screen in front of you, Mr. Djukic, is an RS MUP Bijeljina information report on the situation in Bosanski Samac. The report is dated the 19th of November, 1992. As you can see here in the middle of this page, it says that after Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, was arrested, the Bosanski Samac War Presidency went to the MUP of Serbia with a written request to redeploy Crni and his group to the area where combat operations were taking place. Were you aware of these efforts to request the Serbian MUP to have Crni released from prison and brought back to Bosanski Samac? Yes or no, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kindly understand my position. I had an order where, after my wounding, I had to rejoin the corps on the 30th of November. I know of this event only from what I heard from the officers visiting me in Banja, where I was undergoing treatment. So I kindly ask you not to ask me about this. Whatever has to do with Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, boils down to what I heard from him, that he had arrived from Krajina. And his CV before the arrival in Zabari on the 12th of April is something that I know nothing of, and that's why I didn't give any answers to that. I have no remarks to make on what you've presented here to me because I knew nothing of Djordjevic until I met him; that's to say, before April of 1992, before that part of his life, I knew nothing what was going on there. I knew that there was some misconduct on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, the question simply was whether you were aware of efforts to request the Serbian MUP to have Crni released from prison and brought back to, as the original text says, to -- to the area where combat operations were taking place. Now, I do understand. You say, "I know of this event only from what I heard from the officers visiting me in Banja," where you were undergoing treatment. Do I then understand that you say you knew of these efforts to request the Serbian MUP to have Crni released only because those who came to visit you told you about it and that you have no direct knowledge of that? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to tell you that there was a publication that I made in a manual. And as for the goal of my testimony here, I correctly understood the brochure on page 4. Thirdly, nobody could have gone through to the MUP of Serbia save through private channels to ensure the release of Crni, because it was not within the jurisdiction of the Serbian MUP to have or make sure that somebody who was arrested in this way be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'd like to hear from you is an answer to the question, not what could have happened or could not have happened. Do you have any knowledge of an effort to request the MUP that Crni be released and sent back to the area of combat? Do you have any knowledge, first. Do you have any personal knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say that I'm testifying about what I heard, saw, and what I know, which is a rule that you apply here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, do you have any personal knowledge of such an effort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you hear by visitors of such an effort being made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I please have P1417 again, not to be broadcast, and could I have page 3 in English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, this is back to Crni's statement. As can you see here, he says: "My arrest followed soon after, and I spent about -- around ten days in detention. After my release, Colonel Petar Salapura told me that I had not been arrested but had been put away in a safe place because of an assassination that had been planned against me and offered me to stay in the fight. I did not agree to this, and I went to Yugoslavia to put my thoughts together and come to terms with everything. "While I was at home, the Samac municipality War Staff sent various memos and made phone calls, as did Colonel Salapura and Colonel Novica Simic, via the Serbian state security, requesting my return to Bosnia, with as many men as possible and one special unit. I agreed and arrived in Samac at the beginning of October." Now, Mr. Djukic, I am aware that you were injured at this time. We are aware of that. I'd like to know, did you ever learn of Jovica Stanisic's direct involvement, the Serbian SDB's direct involvement, in the release of Crni?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Salapura is my chief. He was Tolimir's deputy in the main security administration of the Army of Republika Srpska and would never -- he would never stoop so low as to ask -- as to ask Crni to help his army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Petar Salapura is my boss, and he got engaged to find a flat for me in order that I should be able to stay in the army. He was a top-notch officer and later a general, and he would never ask a citizen such as Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, to help him. Again, it would be down to the civilian structures of Bosanski Samac, Blagoje, Simic, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I now invite you to answer the question. The question was whether you ever learned about a direct involvement of Mr. Stanisic in the release of Crni.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know who Jovica Stanisic was at the time, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is you did never learn about his involvement. Then the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- next question was whether you learned anything about the Serbian SDB's direct involvement in the release of Crni. Did you ever learn about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that no one, whether you trust him or not, ever told you about such a thing, and you have no other knowledge about it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus. Or I am looking at the clock. Could I, before we continue, Ms. Marcus, in terms of time, of course, the Chamber has to consider whether or not to extend the session. Could you give us a further estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say two and a half hours, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need, Mr. Petrovic? As matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this time, 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Five minutes, at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Now, 15 plus 5 is 20. Two and a half hours is two sessions of 75 minutes. Therefore, if everyone would be very disciplined, and if no one bothers me during the break with matters which causes delay in returning to this courtroom, and we'll try to avoid that, that two sessions for you, and then 20 minutes would still stay within a last session of one hour and five minutes, instead of 75. If the parties could commit themselves to that, then the Chamber will refrain from organising a session in the second half of the afternoon, or at least to explore the possibility for such a session. I'm looking at all of you. No one seems to jump up and to say, Please explore a further session in the second half of the afternoon. Then we'll proceed that way. And we'll resume at a quarter to 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, I got the impression that you received the results of the measurement of your blood pressure and that I take it from your presence here that it's not prohibitive from -- for continuing; is that correct? We don't need to have the results in -- in numbers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no. The pulse is 96, blood pressure is good. I have 34 more units until it becomes critical. I have taken a beta blocker, so there is no need to slow down proceedings or speed them up on my account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will leave the pace to Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to ask the Court Officer to show two different documents on the left and right of the screen, both the B/C/S versions. We've spoken about it, and I understand it is technically possible, and please not to broadcast them. On one side, could we have P1417, B/C/S page 6. And on the other side P179, B/C/S page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I have the wrong page for P1417. It was supposed to be the signature page. Ah okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, so, Mr. Djukic, you what you see before you on the left side is the statement by Crni that we were looking at before. And on the right side, you see Crni's autobiography which is from his Serbian DB file. That is dated the 25th of February, 1992. Can I draw -- that is this page, this page in that file is of that date. Can I draw your attention to the last line of this paragraph, which states: "I have been on the front since 20th September 1991 and in this unit since 5th October 1991." As you can see by the header, the unit to which he refers is a special purpose unit of the Serbian MUP and the location was Lezimir. Mr. Djukic, isn't it a fact that you were just simply not aware of Crni's membership in the special purposes unit of the Serbian MUP by the time you encountered him in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do object to that question. It's not designed to elicit a fact. The witness isn't away. The reason why he's not aware is not going to be revealed by that question. This has more of the hallmarks of a closing speech designed to show Your Honours the evidence and remind Your Honours of the evidence rather than elicit it from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Marcus, is there any need to confirm at this moment that the witness or with these documents to seek further confirmation that the witness is not aware of -- of -- well, to say the -- the role and the links of Crni with the -- with the -- with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say, you know, the Defence sometimes says we put our case and sometimes says we don't. I'm putting this to the witness. I'm asking him if he has knowledge of it. In my view, Your Honour, respectfully, I think this is perfectly appropriate for cross-examination, and the witness can see it and see whether -- whether -- confirm that he didn't know anything about it. That's our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think, as a matter of fact, that's not the core of the objection by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash says you are not -- what you are doing is to rub in the evidence which you have presented. Now, at the same time, Mr. Jordash, the question, to the extent it seeks to explore whether the witness knows anything or whether he still doesn't know anything when looking at these documents is, of course, in itself not inappropriate. But let's keep it short. Having looked at this, Witness, Mr. Djukic, do you know anything about this, or do you just have no knowledge about the links of Crni with the Republic of Serbia's MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, the question is leading, because it is being suggested that I could know something about it. How would I be able to know it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know something about it, please tell us. Don't comment on the questioning. If the question is irregular, either the Chamber or the Defence will respond to that. Please, I do understand you say, How could I know? I understand that [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that answer to be that you have no knowledge. Yes. Then let's move on Ms. Marcus. By the way, you dated the autobiographic note as the 25th of February, where for me it is the 23rd. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I apologise, Your Honour. Could I then just refer the Chamber to page 1 of P179 which is the request for an operative check of Crni by Mr. Stanisic. I'm done with these documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, before I continue, the document that you offered us to look at, we would indeed like to look at that document when you have a chance. Perhaps maybe with the Chamber's leave, you could hand it to us through the court usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, are you willing to give the document, you'd like one of the parties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one you said earlier you would like, I think the Defence, to have that admitted into evidence. If you give it to the usher, the Prosecution will consider to use it. And if you provide a copy -- or the original. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, there's been evidence in this case that in December of 1992 - that, I believe, is just after your release, first time, from the hospital. There was a report prepared by the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, including some of those individuals whom you identified earlier, including Beronja, Josic, and Maksimovic. And this is a report --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours it's P1418.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- about the -- about what they call a legal elite unit of Serbian commandos, involving Crni, Debeli, and Lugar. And the report says that their presence in Samac had been legalised through official government organs at both the Samac level and the level of the government of Serbia. Now, my question to you is: In your position in the JNA at the time -- in the VRS I should say. At the time, had you not been injured, would you have distanced yourself from Crni, Debeli, and Lugar, as your colleagues did, in fact, would you have distanced yourself, or would you have continued to assert that Crni, Debeli, Lugar were operating under the unique authority of the JNA and then the VRS in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness was not showed a document which has no less than ten pages. But, rather, only a small portion of it and is invited to comment on what he would have done if he were -- if he had been in the shoes of some other individuals and that -- we're talking about document 1418. I invite my learned friend to allow the witness to have a look at the document and then put the question to him. Otherwise, it is not reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be very happy to give the witness a copy of this and to let him read it perhaps over the next break. It is a long one. I was trying to save time. The main point of my question was that there has been evidence that his colleagues distanced themselves, the evidence is in P1418, and I'm asking him whether he would have distanced himself from the activities of Crni, Lugar, and Debeli. I think that's a perfectly legitimate question, but of course I'm very happy to share the document with the witness and see if he would like to add anything later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speed things up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovan Erletic and Milan Miletic have signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that the question can be put to the witness, that the witness can answer the question, but that the witness should be given an opportunity to read the document in its entirety during the next break. And if that causes him to complete or supplement his answer, he'll have an opportunity to do so, but only about the question and not a general comment on the document. So could you please -- the question was whether -- and Ms. Marcus is relying on the evidence which is known to her and which she gave you a very small part, whether you would have distanced yourself from the activities of Crni, Debeli, and Lugar if you would have had the information that was put to you by Ms. Marcus. Could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the order whereby I was deployed as the security organ in the 2nd Bosnia Brigade where Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, through Salapura -- I had to leave Posavina because of Crni and Djordjevic and was appointed as officer in the corps. I distanced myself from them as soon as I could and as far as I could. And I am familiar with this document. I recognised it by its cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, a copy will be given to you, if you want to refresh your memory on that document. We are not seeking your comment on the document but just whether there's anything in that document which would cause you to -- to amend your answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 5603.1; e-court page 256 in English, and page 264 in the original handwritten version. That is, ERN J000-4408. The bottom of the page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, what I'm showing now is a page from the diary of Ratko Mladic. This particular entry records a meeting which Mladic held with the leadership of the Samac municipality on the 7th of December, 1992. As can you see here, Mladic recorded what Stevan Todorovic said: "Sent 18 men to Ilok for training and on 18 April 1992, they were transferred in three" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please have the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: "... three helicopters together with 30 volunteers from Kragujevac; among them, two members of the Serbian MUP, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, and Aleksandar Vukovic. A special battalion was later formed under the command of Crni and it was involved in offensive operations." Mr. Djukic, I'd like to you clearly understand the Prosecution position. Our position is that the accused Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic, through the Serbian DB, trained and armed local Serbs at the Ilok, Pajzos and Lezimir training camps. Simatovic then personally ordered this Red Beret unit to attack Bosanski Samac where they murdered, forcibly transferred, deported, and otherwise persecuted the municipality's non-Serb population in co-ordination with other Serb forces, such as the JNA and the local TO. Now, you are obviously a very respected official, both within the organs you worked for and -- as well as among internationals who worked with you in the region. Can you accept the fact that this connection between the Serbian DB and the events in Bosanski Samac were simply hidden from you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned at some point in time of the crimes committed by Lugar but not on the 7th of May, when he committed them in Crkvine. And it is quite understandable that as a lawyer I cannot condone this act. No one reasonable could do that. But I couldn't know who it was who sent him or who trained that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with this document. Mr. Djukic, I'd like to move onto a different subject now. There has been evidence in this case that about four to six months before the war began, the war in Bosnia, that is, a group of instructors under Captain Dragan arrived in Brcko and formed a special unit which, according to the Brcko War Presidency, made significant contributions to combat operations in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is from P1001, D202, and D83.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This group of instructors included Rade and Bozo Bozic, Simo Radovanovic, and Sasa Vukojevic and operating in co-ordination with them were Goran Petkovic, Zivojin Jovanovic, Ljubisa Savic, Mirko Blagojevic, and Arkan's Men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, D83.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, according to this evidence: During the Brcko takeover, Captain Dragan's instructors and Goran Petkovic and Zivojin Jovanovic, aka Crnogorac, used a self-propelled gun and anti-aircraft machine-guns to storm the Brcko SJB. They held the municipal president and the Chief of Staff of the 1st Posavina Brigade hostage, threatening to liquidate them unless three of their member who had been arrested were released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, P3017.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the information that I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am aware from the priest Slavko Maksimovic, as a source, who himself committed crimes, because he actually tried to convert Muslims to the Orthodox faith. And as I've already said about Zika Jovanovic, Crnogorac, I've already said that I saw him, that he was present in Brcko, and I do not contest their acts and I do feel that justice should be meted out to them because there was a great crime committed there. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer. Could you just repeat the very last part.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no shelling or rocket attacks on the building of the Secretariat of the Interior in Brcko. It stands unchanged to this day where it was 50 years ago. And I omitted -- I also said there may have been threats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now according to this evidence that I've just put to you, certain formations in the Brcko area, including the Serbian Volunteer Guard, Captain Dragan's Red Berets, and Zika Crnogorac were directed to those areas by the Serbian DB.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, P3017.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you like to comment on that briefly, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than the fact that I do not know who sent them, and the fact that based on my knowledge, which is extensive, I never saw any effects as a result of any actions by Captain Dragan and his forces. The main role was played by Dragan Savic, Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of an individual named Zeljko Torbica in relation to the Brcko corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now Mr. Simatovic spoke of the strategic importance of the Posavina corridor himself at an award ceremony at the Kula camp after the war. I'm going to ask Mr. Laugel to play a very brief clip. This is in evidence as P61. The clip is from 15 minutes and 18 seconds to 16 minutes and 41 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: "[VOICEOVER]: In May 1991 an air-helicopter squadron was formed which transported tonnes of special shipments, equipment, troops and machinery from the improvised airfields of Medeno Polje, Petrovac, Velika Popina, Srb, and Udbina and carried out numerous complex tasks while war operations were ongoing. "In September 1991 a part of the unit was transferred to Serbia, where its reconstruction was conducted and high-quality professional training organised. These two units were involved in operations in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. Twenty six training camps for special police units of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were also formed in that period. In the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Golubic, Dinara, Obrovac, Gracac, Plitvice, Sumarice, Petrova Gora, Licki Osik, Benkovac, Lezimir, Ilok, and Vukovar, and in RSK in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Trebinje, Visegrad, Ozren, and Mrkonjic Grad. "Units of Serbian joint operations in Eastern Slavonia, the corridor at Brcko, in the Drina, Sarajevo, and Maglaj operations. In western Bosnia, the unit was the backbone of Fikret Abdic's army with around 1500 [as interpreted] soldiers who freed most of Cazin Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, did you have a -- Mr. Djukic, you have testified that you were not aware of the relationship between the Serbian DB and events in Bosanski Samac. Isn't it a fact you were also not aware of the Serbian DB's involvement in the Brcko operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't want to waste time with unnecessary objections, but this is not designed to elicit fact. It's designed to continuously play evidence and show evidence to Your Honours and to the witness and then say -- ask the witness questions which do not add anything to what we've already seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, to establish that the witness doesn't know something, then it's -- you don't have to show all the evidence, although it may be to some extent be triggered to -- by the Stanisic Defence now and then that we should be clear to the witness. But I think that, under the present circumstances, if you seek confirmation of the lack of knowledge of the witness, it could be done in -- without showing all of that evidence to him. You could have summarised what was said in two or three lines without showing the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the witness just answer that question, Your Honour, about --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My question was: Isn't it a fact that you were also not aware of the Serbian DB's involvement in the Brcko corridor operations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. I didn't know about that. But I have to say that this video-clip is very familiar, and it is my view that these officers here are just bragging before President Milosevic. I saw this videotape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about your knowledge, not to comment on the video. Although that, of course, Ms. Marcus, is a risk if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, but I was shown this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you are not invited to comment on it but, rather, to answer the question that was put to you. Ms. Marcus, that's, of course, also one of the risks by showing the evidence to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with the witness's comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's -- they seem not to be very relevant at this moment, and -- and they take time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now there's been evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, P1075.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- that from the beginning of the war in 1991, a number of paramilitary units were engaged in the territory of the RSK and the RS. They were and remained in direct contact with the republican state security and the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia or they were engaged under the guise of special units of the republican state security or the Ministry of Interior. Mr. Djukic, this refers, in particular -- this particular piece of evidence refers to Arkan's Men, Vaso Mijovic's men, and the Red Berets under the command of Zika Ivanovic, also known as Crnogorac, and it also refers to the paramilitary unit of Slobodan Medic, aka Boca. Now you've given evidence about Zika Ivanovic and also about Slobodan Medic. This evidence, as well as other evidence in the case, describes criminal activities carried out by Zika Crnogorac. Now what you told us about Zika Crnogorac was that in your view he was involved in investigating and combatting criminal activity. Isn't it a fact that Zika Crnogorac was directly involved in just the criminal activity that you described him cracking down on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the detention of some people that he ordered were unlawful. And Zika Crnogorac currently lives in the United States of America where he had sought asylum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just appreciate if in this Exhibit P1075, if we could be shown this exhibit to see where it talks about the crimes committed by Zika Crnogorac because I may have not seen it. Perhaps my learned friend can show it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you a page indication for Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Page 2 in English, page 2 in B/C/S, Your Honours. I think Mr. Petrovic is free to look at it and find those parts and use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am looking at it, but I can't see any facts about any crimes. That's exactly what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It says: "Some of the more famous individuals will be removed and will work from behind the scenes: Rajo Bozovic, Zika Crnogorac, Zvezdan Jovanovic, Vasilije Mijovic, and so on. Our sources worn that in these units there are professional killers, terrorists, Legionnaires, hardened criminals, and that they are ready to carry out the most callous terrorist operations for money." There are other parts about collecting debts, robbery, smuggling, the liquidation of undesirables. The whole report is basically about the activities of Zika Crnogorac and other units that are described in the report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check that. Meanwhile, we -- what you just read is not a direct indication of Zika Crnogorac committing crimes, but from what you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Not him alone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what you read. From what you read.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I will check in P1075.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please call up P1077.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now what you see before you is a VJ security organ report dated 18th November, 1992. I realise that this was just about at the time when you were dealing with your injury. Could I give you a minute to look through the document, and I will ask you just a couple of questions about Zika Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read it. It is a bit smudged. The ends are smudged. I still can't read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You still cannot, even if it would be further enlarged, which is I think still possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Djukic, this document indicates that Arkan and Zvezdan Jovanovic, Zika Crnogorac are "registered criminals." Involved in criminal activity of "big proportions." It says they are "closely connected with the top leaders of the MUP of Serbia," including Stanisic and Kostic and the government of the SBWS, Hadzic, Kojic, and other. Now, you testified that Zika Crnogorac came to the "secretariat, asking do look at the files of more expensive luxury cars and some other items which had been illegally taken from well-off Muslim houses." Isn't it a fact that he was coming to take those items for himself and his associates, rather than to investigate those who had taken them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answer briefly. Zika Crnogorac when he saw me said that everything that he had seized, including gold, he took personally to Pale, to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm finished with this document. Thank you. Now you have testified about your participation in the arrest of certain individuals in the area of Ilok, beginning in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's page 17971.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that after the Red Berets left Ilok to participate in combat operations in the area of the Posavina corridor, only a few Red Berets remained in Ilok, headed by Ilija Vuckovic, aka Rambo, to guard Pajzos. A simple yes or no will do. I understand the issues you raised yesterday, and we will proceed to private session, if need be. But a simple yes or no at this point will suffice.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I'm not afraid of criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow, again we have a complex question that implies two questions; the first part and the second part. There is an implication here that the witness knows that Red Berets had left Ilok for the corridor. I don't know what the foundation for that question is. First of all, is the witness aware of that, and then he should be asked whether he knew what was going on; otherwise, we are at a risk of receiving an answer to the second portion of the question, and then later on when we look back at it, we might -- it might be implied that he also answered to the first part of the question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, you should have refrained from commenting on the question in the way you did. But Ms. Marcus is invited to split up the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I'd like to just say in response is that I've put a number of series of facts to the witness, and I think the witness has demonstrated clearly his ability to pick out which parts he knows, which parts doesn't, and to comment on those different parts. In this particular instance, I'm asking him some preliminary questions, and then I will put some -- put a document to him. But, Your Honour, I'm -- honestly, I think there is nothing wrong with the facts that I put to him, asking him, Isn't it a fact. He can say whether he knows or doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then if you give three facts then there is a risk that the witness may not have dealt with all three of them. That is what often happened. So would you please put it -- I think the -- for example whether Red Berets remained, whether they were headed by. I mean, that could be easily misunderstood. Would you please split up the question and make it separate items.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, isn't it a fact that after the Red Berets left Ilok to participate in combat operations, a few remained behind in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, nor is it possible. You didn't allow me yesterday to explain. In Ilok there was an UNPROFOR Russian battalion, the peacekeeping forces, that would expelled such -- driven away such units immediately, even had we not wanted to -- wanted them to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please not tell us what was possible or was not possible, but would you please tell us about facts. Is it true or not true that, when the Red Berets left Ilok that a few remained behind? I'm not talking about units, I'm not talking about who should have spotted them. Is that true or not; or do you not know? Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the question? I believe the problem here is that I'm not allowed to explain anything. I mean, in this way, nothing will be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could leave that to the parties and to the Chamber. The question was whether, when the Red Berets left Ilok, whether a few of them remained behind. Whether that's true, whether that's not true, or whether you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise, as of 15th March, 1993, there were no Red Berets present in Ilok. Before that point, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know whether when they left whether anyone remained behind because you say, I arrived at a time where they had left, if they have ever been there already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I have just one brief moment, sir. Could the Court Officer please call up P3042 but not to broadcast it to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, this is a report by the JATD of the Serbian SDB from the 1st of February 1994. If relates to the activities in Ilok in the period from 15 to 30th of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I please have page two in English and page 16 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
