utterances.text: What it says on the page in front of us is that: "In order to paint a more detailed picture of the Red Berets' actions in this area, we have to go back to the 1992 period; namely, after the opening of the corridor. The Republic of Serbia MUP unit that was in this area was practically disbanded. Only a small number remained, headed by Ilija Vuckovic, aka Rambo, to guard the Pajzos and Bela Kuca. The group styled itself in the Red Berets image, which term was subsequently used in an increasingly negative context. In the course of 1992, almost all its members had wilfully abandoned the unit or were expelled from it due to various reasons. A majority of them found sanctuary in Ilok and continued doing dirty jobs, using the uniform and insignia of the Red Berets." A bit further down it says: "Apart from two registered cases of unauthorised hunting, objectively speaking, some members of our unit can be criticised for improper and arrogant behaviour and inappropriate use of Republic of Serbia MUP registered vehicles, but this is not subject to criminal or misdemeanour prosecution."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I please request private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Djukic, often you say I'll stick to your rules, I'll not explain further. If the explanation would change the core of your answer, then, of course, you're supposed to do that because you are supposed to give the whole truth. Now, we are not inviting you to comment on things you are not asked, but if the answer by a yes or a no would be misleading, then, of course, you're invited to add as much as to create the right picture. Not a full understanding of situation. I'll just give you one example. I asked you about -- where you said that Zika had investigated the stolen vehicles, or that he -- he came and wanted to see the files. Then I asked you what was the purpose? Was that to investigate? And then you said -- you said that he wanted to investigate that. I asked what it then resulted in. You said certain investigations were conducted. Cases were processed so that those files or cases would appear before the International Tribunal. Well, then I asked you so the purpose was to investigate and to prosecute those who had stolen those vehicles. And you confirmed that that was your answer. Now, today you told us that he took the cars and brought them to Karadzic, which is, of course, not the usual way of investigating and prosecuting because in that context there's no place for taking the seized vehicles to the -- to the president of -- of a republic. So, therefore, at that moment, where you felt free to tell us about an appointment you had, et cetera, et cetera. You wanted to add quite a lot of things there and I didn't interrupt you. But there you should have said, The purpose was to investigate; however, in reality, he took the seized cars and brought them to Pale. That is what I would have expected you to do because your answer: Investigation, prosecution, that, of course, is only half of the picture, because, in that picture, it doesn't fit that you take the cars and bring them to Pale. So, therefore, that was something we would have expected you to add, not whether you had an appointment next week with someone else to talk about these kind of things. May that be clear that as long as what you'd like to add is there to give the right picture where your answer did not give a right picture, then you're not only allowed but even under an obligation to do that. You may proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, Jovan Kujundzic was appointed command in Pajzos on the 11th of June, 1992. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to 1992 and Ilok, please do not put questions to me. It is futile because it's already well-known that I arrived in the area on 15th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, were you aware that there were many individuals who were affiliated with the Serbian MUP but also held ID cards of the Krajina MUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across an official who would have held an ID of both the RSK MUP and the Serbian MUP. Admittedly, Mladic [as interpreted] would give away lightly to drivers or whomever the official IDs and almost everyone was in possession of one such ID card.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P489. In the meantime, can I just refer the Chamber to P3017 for the prior question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I -- at the same time, could I seek clarification of your last answer. You said: "Admittedly, Mladic would give away lightly to drivers or whomever the official IDs ..." Official IDs of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry that you misunderstood. That it had to with Martic. Martic. Mladic was an honest officer until 1992, who would not have given anything lightly to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Martic. Were you then referring to giving Krajina MUP IDs given by Martic to drivers and the other persons you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He would give some of those as a souvenir, even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see in front of you is a list of Serbian MUP personnel who have ID cards of the Krajina MUP. At the top of the list you see Zika Crnogorac. And at number 42 you see Jovan Kujundzic whom I mentioned earlier. Now our position is that the men who remained in Ilok Pajzos, including Jovan Kujundzic and Ilija Vuckovic, were in fact part of the Serbian DB. The fact that they signed documents on JPN Krajina letterhead, in our view, does not change the fact that they were in fact JPN Serbia members. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, my learned friend mischaracterised the evidence. She said what you see here is a list of the Serbian MUP personnel. Could my learned friend show where it says in the document that this is a list of the Serbian MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Marcus put the OTP interpretation of this list, a list apparently containing what she considers to be members of the MUP. Now, apart from summarising the document, it has been emphasised again and again that the Prosecution should put to the witness what their case is in this respect. Perhaps, Ms. Marcus, it would have been better to say that what you see in front of you is a list containing names of Serbian MUP personnel. So it's not said by Ms. Marcus, at least I take it that you did not intend to say, that all of these are MUP of Serbia members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this moment I was just referring to the two that I'm mentioning and I'm going to show additional evidence for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were invited to comment on the two persons of which the Prosecution says they were MUP of the Republic of Serbia employees appearing on this list, apparently having been given MUP of the Krajina -- if you not mind that I finish my question. Appearing on this list of people having IDs of the -- of the RSK MUP. Please comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, I don't see the date. Secondly, this is very important. The Serbian MUP contained public and state security. Security service and state security -- that's to say, public security and state security would be held accountable separately. So we ought to know, first, under which branch these people fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue raised by Ms. Marcus is what is the explanation for Serbian MUP employees, irrespective of what branch, to be issued with Krajina MUP IDs. That's the issue. It's Serbia against Krajina; rather than state security, public security. Any further comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Krajina MUP would easily give ID cards; whereas, the Serbian MUP never issued a colleague of mine with an official ID card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P3038 and not broadcast it to the public. P3038. And I'd like page 15 in English and page 13 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, this is the DB, Serbian DB personnel file for Ilija Vuckovic. As you can see on this document, Ilija Vuckovic was a member of the reserve forces of the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Interior, from the 5th of May, 1991, to the 1st of November, 1992. Now, our position is that both Ilija Vuckovic and Jovan Kujundzic were carrying out their activities in Pajzos as official members of the JPN of the Serbian MUP in spite of the fact that they may also have been signing documents on JPN Krajina MUP letterhead. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document is valid. However, it is a bit odd. When I brought him in and the court remanded him in custody in Beli Manastir, it is a bit odd that Serbia failed to protect its member, if he, indeed, was their member.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that document. Now, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the man you identified as your superior, Ilija Kojic. At page 18008 you said this about Ilija Kojic: "His role was totally clear. Kojic was an official, a public official. He was a representative of the ministry before other competent organs. He would approve all our contacts with the public media. He was in charge of material and logistical security and in charge of other duties, such as contacts with various assemblies, with the commands, and similar." Can you tell us, first, what you meant by material and logistical security? As briefly as possible, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say was that Ilija Kojic was in terms of logistics very much capable of providing us with vehicles, food, and the rest. Unfortunately, we never received these items from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now what did you mean when you said that Kojic was "in charge of other duties, such as contacts with various assemblies, with the commands, and similar"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applies to presidents of assemblies, because quite a few assemblies were put together. For instance, in Tenja and Mirkovci there was a great deal of arrogance exhibited on their part, and he negotiated with them as well as with Loncar, because I told him that I was not in contact with the Army of Krajina. Now when I saw these intercept, I felt really in a way disappointed as an officer and a human being yesterday here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you clarify your last comment. You said, "When I saw these intercepts I felt in a way disappointed as an officer and a human being." Briefly, what -- what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they are accurate, then General Loncar lied to me, and he should take his rightful place alongside the war crimes prosecutor. Loncar is, who, as you will know, is very efficient and expeditious in processing war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At page 18009, you said of Mr. Kojic: "He was, for all practical purposes, minister in the absence of Minister Martic." Is it fair to say that Mr. Kojic was the most powerful official in the Ministry of Interior in the SBWS when Martic was not present?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the district of Eastern Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem is concerned, since he was the head of the TO for that district, he was seriously wounded, barely escaped with his life, and he was highly esteemed by the population there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know that he was wounded and esteemed. But the question was what power he had. And I take it that Ms. Marcus was not focussing on the time when he was seriously wounded. Was he, when he was in function, the second powerful person, as -- when Mr. Martic wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I knew of him at the time, I would not have accepted him as a superior of mine, someone who has secondary education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But was he the second as far as power is concerned? Whether you like his education or not, it was not the question. The question was whether he was the second, after Martic, if it comes to power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was number two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And Martic was not present most of the time in SBWS; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic would come to Eastern Slavonia periodically, because, and quite understandably so, he had to cover Krajina, which wasn't large in itself, but between Borovo and Knin there's 650 kilometres, and it was difficult to cover it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At page 18049, Mr. Jordash asked the following question: "In late 1994, early 1995, when these operations were ongoing, did Martic ever charge his view about the Serbian DB? Did he suddenly start to express trust in them, or was he always someone to regarded the likes of Kojic and Kostic a problem?" Your answer was: "I really cannot understand that. They were close friends. They spoke on a number of occasions. For instance, when I went to Ilok, sometimes I would even sit at a different table. They would sit at another table, which I didn't mind at all. From what I could observe myself, they had a very good relationship mutually, and he even continued this relation with Kojic when Dalmacija fell. Kojic offered all kinds of assistance to him." Then you were asked: "To whom, sorry?" And your answer was: "To Martic." Can you tell us what kind of assistance Kojic offered to Martic, to your knowledge? Briefly, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He offered that he should resettle with his family and that they would ensure the basic provisions for his family and that if he needed a job, he was ready to provide him with one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is it correct that Ilija Kojic was your superior from the time you arrived in SBWS in March 1993 through to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through to the end of the war, with one remark: Minister Martic would consult with me frequently, one on one. He even asked me to advise him on whether he should run for the president. He also asked me to use the personal form of address with him, to give him the Tu, as it were, which I always refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless I've lost track of time, if this is the time for the break then this could be a good stopping point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is the time for the break. Before we take that break, however, Mr. Jordash, I announced that we would consider either a late afternoon session, but we more or less agreed that it should be possible to conclude the evidence in of this witness in a 105 minutes' session. Of course, that goes beyond what the doctors have advised. So I'd like to hear from you whether Mr. Stanisic wants, then, to be absent, or whether he insists not to continue, which, of course, is -- he is entitled to -- to be present at his trial. So if that would cause any problem, then I'd like to know. By the way, a later afternoon session would also be in -- not consistent with the advice of the doctors, and, therefore if there's any problem there I'd like to know so that we can adjust plans, if need be, to the position of the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear from you immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if it changes the dramatically plans, I would even like to be informed during the break so that we can take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Stanisic apparently is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can continue, Your Honours, and Mr. Stanisic would like to return to the UNDU, if he can, and he waives his right to be present during the final parts of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only the final 30 minutes but already now? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I inform Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's document I promised to show the witness if -- during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it could be given to the witness by the usher. Something for you to read, Mr. Djukic, during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Homework again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We could do an extended session with Mr. Stanisic present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll resume at 12.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, until quarter to 2.00, the time is yours. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic at page 18027, you were asked whether you were aware of any relationship between Ilija Kojic and the DB of Serbia. And you said: "I don't, nor was I told, nor do you ask such things of your colleagues?" I'd like to look at that in a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can we please have P325 on the screen but not broadcast it to the public. P325. And could I have, please, page 7 of the English and page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, if you take a look at this document, you'll see that it has the heading of the state security sector of the Republic of Serbia and that it is dated 19th of March, 1993. So it's the time of your arrival in the SBWS. And now I'll read verbatim the portion following the word "decree." It says: "Ilija Kojic, employed at the Ministry of Interior, the secretariat in Belgrade: "Is deployed starting from 1 April 1993 to the working place from Article 11, item 7, of the rule-book on systemisation of workplaces of the sector of state security in the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. "The title of the employee will be independent clerk." And if we go to the bottom of the page in B/C/S and the middle of the next page in English, we can see that the document is signed and stamped by Jovica Stanisic as chief. Sir, were you really not aware that Ilija Kojic was an employee of the State Security Department of Serbia at the time that he was your boss?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about contacts, I meant contacts in the operative sense. It doesn't mean private contacts. Now if you're asking me whether I knew that he was on the payroll of Serbia, I wouldn't know. According to this decision, Ilija Kojic was a secret agent of the Serbian MUP in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry just in terms of your last answer, part of it you said, "Now if you're asking me" -- this is what the transcript says. I just want to correct the transcript or -- verify that it was correct. You said: "Now if you're asking me whether I was on the payroll of Serbia, I wouldn't know." Did you mean to say, "Now if you're asking me whether he was on the payroll of Serbia..."? Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had I known - and we worked together, we risked our lives together - had I known that he was on the Serbian payroll, whereas I was on this miserable pay in Krajina, I wouldn't have worked with him together. Now according to this decision, which is not usual, it would appear that he infiltrated our ranks which was not uncommon in intelligence circles, and he most certainly would not have told us about it or anybody else because that would have caused a lot of discontent among us. So, in other words, I think this was really not very fair of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. Now you also testified about Rade Kostic. You mentioned that he came with Martic to visit you when the shrapnel was removed to offer you a position. And then you also said at page 18009 to 18010: "We dealt with serious matters and Kostic was this charge of the entire territory; whereas, Kojic was only in charge of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." The question then was: "What do you mean Kostic was in charge of the entire territory? Which territory are you including within that?" And your answer was: "The Republic of Serbian Krajina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the first portion of the question was misquoted. It says that Martic and Kostic offered the witness something, and I don't think that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- you mean the quoted part which is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this part when it reads: "You mentioned that he came with Martic to visit you when the shrapnel was removed to offer you a position." I believe that that part of the transcript was not put correctly to the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus. Now, it seems to be -- by the way, it seems to be a marginal aspect of and doesn't affect the question in any way. But, nevertheless, I agree with you, Mr. Petrovic, that quotes -- reference to evidence should be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, yes. At page 1769 and 70 the witness spoke about a visit he received from Martic and Kostic, and he does say it's true that Martic was making the offer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that has now been corrected. Then perhaps you repeat your question so that the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, should I repeat the quote that I put to him from -- I hadn't asked the question yet. I was putting a quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need to repeat the quote. The problem was just in the introductory part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on whether the witness still remembers. That's the issue, and not whether you oppose, Mr. Petrovic. Could you please resume, Ms. Marcus, in the way you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, do you remember the question I put to you? I quoted to your statement that Kostic was in charge of the entire territory of Republic of Serbian Krajina. Now my question to you is: Did you ever have any indication that Kostic, who was, as you say, in charge of the entire territory of the RSK, was actually working for the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, already at the hospital, by just looking at him, at his gestures and the faces he was making, I knew that he was against my going there. He was very arrogant to me. He never had a coffee with me. He would just come in and we would exchange greetings and then he would say -- he always had this yellow bag with him, he would always rush off somewhere. He would say he was in a hurry, and I always warned him that he shouldn't really hurry so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not answer the question, Mr. Djukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the question? Perhaps I -- it slipped my mind. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether -- did you have any -- did you ever have any indication that Kostic was actually working for the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought that it was implicit from what I said that we were not very close, and I never talked to him about that, nor did I have any indications other than the fact that his wife worked somewhere in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have P406. And could I ask, please, for page 3 in B/C/S and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the heading on this document, we can see it is dated --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. If -- just -- perhaps I'm being overly anticipatory, but if what my learned friend is going to do is again just show -- the witness has said he doesn't know. Now my learned friend, it looks as though she's going to show him what is a state security record, and then with a raised eyebrow say, Are you sure you didn't know. It's just another attempt to bring the evidence before Your Honours. If my learned friend wants to read that evidence, Your Honours, I won't object to that, but we should try to save time, respectfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you see Mr. Jordash is offering his assistance. Why not say to the witness, Would your answer be the same even if I would show you documentary evidence which links him to the Serbian DB. And then the witness can answer the question and we move on. I mean, we don't have to convince this witness that there was a link, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm happy to leave it there, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, this is what, I take it, repeat the question, saying there's even documentary evidence presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. And we've already indicated we agree that this record is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Marcus. And perhaps because this is, of course, a repetition. It's not the first time that Mr. Jordash is on his feet. I think I earlier gave you already guidance that it could be dealt with in a more simple way. So would you please keep that in mind if you have any future documents to show to the witness after he has testified that he doesn't know anything about A, B, or C. Rather leave it to that or one additional question. If I would show you documentary evidence on A, would you still ... and then move on. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that after the war the DB of Serbia maintained a training camp or base for the JSO Kula and that that training centre was named for Rade Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, P61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew of that. And even as of chief of service, because of the name I gave them as a gift - and I was authorised to do that - a vehicle because I felt -- I thought that these were honourable men. I made a mistake. I'm sorry, I was misled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you clarify what you said. You said you gave them a gift. You said, "I them as a gift, I was authorised to do that, a vehicle." Can you tell us who you gave that vehicle to and who authorised you to give it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the authorised person. I was the chief of service. After Kojic left on the 27th of April 1996, all the burdens because of our poor equipment, the poor equipment of the public security, was my burden, and I had to go around begging for money for salaries to pay out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, why not answer the question: To whom was that vehicle given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the training centre in Kula, Rade Kostic. Because I thought that this was an elite honourable unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, then isn't it possible that others could have had a relationship with the Serbian DB that you also didn't know about, such as Martic and such as Slobodan Medic, Boca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boca - and I've already explained this - and Milanovic had ties with the public security of Serbia. That's not in dispute. But very few services would want to have Martic as their collaborator.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I just ask my question again. Isn't it possible that others could also have had a relationship with the Serbian DB that you may not have known about. Those others, including Martic, including Boca, including Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I've said that Milanovic and Boca had ties with Badza - Radovan Stojicic, in other words - and with Rodja, the chief of the public security department, not the state security. I knew about that. That was Vlastimir Djordjevic, also known as Rodja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Just one more time I will ask you the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, the problem in the question is that the witness says that he had some awareness of links of two of the persons you mentioned. So we should then focus the question on the remainder. Now, you told us that Milanovic and Boca you knew had ties with Badza. Now, the question has not been answered in relation to Martic. You said I -- most services, few services would want to have him as their collaborator. Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Is it your testimony that you have no knowledge of Martic having such links to the Serbian DB and which you would not know of and that you consider that it is unlikely that he had on the basis of your assessment of Mr. Martic and how useful such a person would be for a service? Is that we will understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's well understood. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'd like to then deal with the remainder of the question. That is, is it possible that other persons may have had links with the Serbian DB but that you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a collaborator is a person who in a organised manner and secretly and permanently provides information to some service. Now, how would I know when it's secret? Had they offered it to me, I would have accepted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say it is possible that these things would have been the case without me knowing it. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that the relation between Kojic and Martic was generally good, and we agree with that. But there was a point at which tension developed briefly in that relationship and that was around the time that Ilija Prijic was kidnapped; is that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct. The abduction scenario, or, rather, his removal from the public security, and that's a legitimate act, I was in favour of him being removed from our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Around the end of August 1994, RSK minister of the interior Ilija Prijic publicly stated at a press conference that he been kidnapped by four paramilitary soldiers in Borovo Selo, put into a car, and released several hours later in a forest near Bijeljina. He publicly accused Radislav Kostic of being behind the kidnapping and also publicly said that Radislav Kostic worked for the Serbian state security. That's all correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I selected, I hand-picked the police members who would arrest him. He was not injured. He was taken to a wood near Bijeljina. And on his person, he had a huge amount of foreign currency, of money. These police officers never took a penny from that. He is now living in Belgrade, and he has a police academy or something. We were in fact very gentle with him in view of what he would have deserved, in fact. But first we asked Martic to allow us to remove him from that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, why not answer the question? The question was whether, at the end of August 1994, that the RSK minister of the interior publicly stated that he had been kidnapped by four paramilitary soldiers in Borovo Selo. Did he say so at a press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never read anything about that. I never found that anywhere to read. I read an article that he wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- and did he say in that article that he was kidnapped by four paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I had -- hadn't read anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that I then misunderstood. Are you aware of any public accusation by him that Rade Kostic was behind the kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of it, and I went to the editorial office of "Vjesnik" on Wednesday in order to -- to offer a denial of that. I don't know why it was never published, but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was it also then publicly said that Radovan Kostic worked for the Serbian state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what he also said at a meeting. It was a very difficult meeting. I tried to appease everyone around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: okay. That answers the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say "he also said that at a meeting," who said -- who said what at a meeting? Just so that I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic presided over the meeting, and I -- I reported and we appealed that Minister -- which appealed to him that Minister Prijic be removed because the service -- the officers who were in that service were very dissatisfied with his work, and he left Croatia on the 1st of January, 1993. But Martic did not accept that. After this, his security detail cocked their weapons, and then I assessed, and this -- we were in office number 10 there, we assessed, I said that he should be removed from there, and -- because there was a possibility that someone would get shot and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could we take the witness back to one of his previous answers. So you say Mr. Martic said that Mr. Kostic was -- at least there was a hint that he was working for the Serbian DB. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No you misunderstood me. Mr. Prijic. That was what the question was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he hinted with Mr. Kostic being -- being linked to the RDB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible. And I can just add that the late Kostic was born in Serbia, so no wonder if he worked for his country. I was paid to work for a foreign country and I refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But whether it's true or not is another matter. What I would like you to -- I asked you, and I'll go to it again, I asked you: "Now was it also then publicly said that Radovan Kostic worked for the Serbian state security?" And you said: "Yes, that's what he also said at a meeting." When I then asked you about Mr. Martic saying so, you said, "No, it was not Mr. Martic. It was Mr. Prijic." Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, earlier you were asked, did you have ever -- did you have any indication that Kostic was actually working for the DB of Serbia, and your answer was a bit unclear. And then I asked you again to answer the question. I said: "Did you ever have any indication that Kostic was actually working for the DB of Serbia?" You said: "I apologise. I thought it was implicit from what I said that we were not very close and I never talked to him about it, nor did I have any indications other than the fact that his wife worked somewhere in Belgrade." What you say the only thing that could hint at Kostic being working for the DB would be the fact that his wife was working in Belgrade, which is not a very strong indication, to say the least. And now you tell us -- half an hour later, you tell us that it was publicly said by Prijic that Kostic was working for the DB. Isn't that an indication of him working for the DB, if someone says so in public? Yes, you may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't find Prijic's words relevant. He was an individual we wanted to remove from the position of minister. I told you that it nearly came to a blows and armed conflict. I told you that there was no information like that going around the service. If he was an agent or a collaborator, that was something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An indication isn't yet a fact. If you consider the mere fact that his wife was working in Belgrade worth mentioning, then certainly a public statement, whether or not you believed it or not, whether you considered it a reliable indication or not is a different matter, should have been part of your answer and you should not have kept it away from us and then later to say, I considered it not to be relevant, or it was an indication. Although, as I understand, you didn't believe it at the time, although it would not surprise you. And whether it's true or not, is another matter. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to ask you briefly about the incident in October of 1994 when Martic was stopped at the border crossing between Serbia and the RSK. At page 18031, you were asked about this incident. The question was: "Do you know anything about Martic's complaint at this time complaining that Kojic and Kostic were effectively acting against his interests, including having their men stop him it the Tovarnik crossing?" Your answer was: "These weren't Kojic's or Kostic's men. This was the check-point unit, and there was an oversight on their part. They did not recognise the minister right away." Now, first of all, in October 1994, Milan Martic was not minister. He was the president of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that he was president. It is also true that members of the police were responsible for this oversight. But his security detail made an error, too, because they should have announced his passage through. There's always a patrol going ahead of them, reporting which patrol point they were at at any given time, which was not the case in this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Milan Martic was one of the most famous people in the RSK, since 1990 or 1991, by the time of this event. Would you agree? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. I told you that as an individual who held the most responsibility for the police saw this to be a gross oversight and irresponsible conduct on the part of the policemen who failed to recognise their president, and they were no longer allowed to perform these tasks. They were transferred to tasks of a lower responsibility and were replaced by individuals who were up to that task and who knew at least one foreign language.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I please have P987 on the screen. This is one of the documents that was shown to you by the Defence. Could I please have the middle of page 2 in English, and the bottom half of page 1 in B/C/S. Can I call your attention to the portion which says -- by the way, to remind you this is a letter from Milan Martic to Slobodan Milosevic regarding this incident at the border. "At the crossing, I was met by Colonel Stojan Spanovic, corps Chief of Staff, who was in a military... car. He got into my car and immediately informed me that the crossing on the RSK side was under the control of Ilija Kojic's men. Our column consisted of a VRSK Ford with a rotating light, an Audi in which I was, and a Mitsubishi Pajero with my escort. When we arrived at the crossing, we were flagged down. As we pulled up a dozen or so men wearing military camouflage uniforms came up to our cars with their rifles points, fingers on the triggers. They were weapons were pointed both at me personally and at all my men." Could we now please have the middle of page 3 in English and the top of page two in B/C/S. I'll read the portion beginning with the words "At the meeting..." "At the meeting in the command of the 11th Corps in Vukovar, I was given the following information. The men who organised the incident were members of the paramilitary and parapolice forces stationed in Erdut. They are under the direct control of Rade Kostic of the State Security Department of the MUP of Serbia. These individuals also took part in the kidnapping of Ilija Prijic, minister of the interior of the RSK. "The said Rade Kostic had entered the territory of the RSK an hour before I did, i.e., at about 0900 hours, in an official BMW with registration plates of the MUP of Serbia. "The command of the 11th VRSK Corps has no authority whatsoever over the camp in Erdut or any other in Eastern Slavonia or Baranja." Sir, there wasn't a simple mixup, was it? This was, in fact, a way of reminding Martic who held the real power in the SBWS, the same way that Ilija Prijic had been reminded when he tried to suspend Kojic and Kostic; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the authority to assess the decisions taken by Kojic or Kostic. I was given a detailed report on this by Dragan Djukic who was the secretary of the Vukovar SUP and who was referred in connection with the incident when Arkan stormed into the SUP. I accepted it. It is possible that I didn't know of it, that I wasn't informed of it, but believe me when I tell that you I speak the truth. I do allow for the possibility that this incident did, indeed, happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that document. Could I now please have P1605 on the screen. Sir, this is the text of an intercepted conversation between Martic and someone identified as the president, who we say is Slobodan Milosevic. The conversation is from 4 October 1994, three days before the letter we were just looking at. At the beginning of the conversation, Martic introduces himself and asks to speak to the president. If we could have the bottom of the page in English, please. I will now read a portion, beginning with the words, "Mr. President hello?" As I read, the letter M represents things said by Martic, while the letter X represents things said by the president, President Milosevic. "M: Mr. President, hello. "X: Hello. "M: I am calling from Vukovar. You know what? I have gone through such an embarrassment. This is not to be tolerated. "X: Pardon me? "M: The very same gang that was carrying out arrests before, from Erdut, waited for me with rifles pointed at me and carried out a search vehicle by vehicle. "X: Did what? "M: They waited for me, around 15 of them. With rifles pointed at me, and ... from vehicle to vehicle, did they think perhaps that ... but such a behaviour, please, either you will order Jovica to withdraw this gang or I will deal with it my way. Believe me, I will run them over with tanks, whatever the outcome. I am kindly asking you. This has gone beyond limits. Kostic, the one who was removed passed this way an hour ago and organised them to come and wait for me with rifles pointed and to maltreat me. Mr. President, I believe that definitely this is definitely not to be tolerated. "X: Absolutely. "M: If you have any respect for me, you will order Jovica Stanisic, who is pulling the strings, to remove this gang from here within one or two hours time, not to see them here ever again, or in Erdut, Pajzos, (?)...," there is a question mark after the word "Pajzos" in the English, "... or wherever it is that they have encamped. That is a true gang, I guarantee you that. "X: And where did they wait for you? "M: Here in Tovarnik, they waited for me, around 15 of them, with rifles pointed at me. The one with a red beret said his name was Marko Bajic. I did not see that. He could have told me any name, but it is the same gang that kidnapped Prijic. I am kindly asking you to order Jovica Stanisic to cleanse them from Erdut, Pajzos, and all other places that they have occupied within an hour or two, otherwise I will have to do something. This is not good." Sir, once again, there is simply no way that this was a mistake. This was a message sent to Milan Martic to remind him that while Serbia supported him, he could not depart too far from the course the Serbian leadership wanted him to follow. In particular, he could not suspend the members of the Serbian DB who worked in his Ministry of the Interior. Isn't that the real truth?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely believe in this. Martic who was the sort of people who would never steer clear of the truth. But let me tell that you this terrible incident was not something that I was aware of, and why would I have been aware of everything, because I was going -- touring the area, because I had to attend to my duties, and I may have well been investigating a murder on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're doing approximately the same as you did before. The witness testified that he received reports that this whole incident about not recognising Martic. Now you may have or may not have doubts about that, but then to ask the witness, Isn't this what happened, which means that -- there are two possibilities: Either there's an assumptions that the witness has any knowledge apart from what was reported to him, that's one option; the other option is that the witness was not telling us the truth when he told us about what was reported to him. Now, these two matters are -- may be relevant to explore, but to say isn't it -- this is what happened, that is a -- I mean, the witness wasn't present, so he has no firsthand knowledge of it. So he relies on reports. And he doesn't know anything about this apparently, about this telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've understood, respectfully, on this particular issue, as far as I understood the witness saying, he did have direct involvement. He said he sent his guys to border in terms of Prijic, and so with his direct involvement and his assertions that would have gone unanswered -- now, I take Your Honours' point. Perhaps one document would have done it. I think one document led him to say it was possible, but because of the point that he had made about this and because of our case on this, I felt that it was my obligation to put to our complete position though this evidence to make sure that he responded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but to put your position to a witness is not the same as to put every piece of evidence to a witness. You could say, We have a -- a telephone conversation recorded in which this and this is said. But the main issue is whether you sent someone there, yes or no. The knowledge of the witness is exclusively based on what was reported to him. Now, whether it was a wrong report or whether the witness has not told us the truth about what was reported to him. That's the key issue, I would say. And what has happened, apparently there is at least contradicting evidence on what has happened, and the Chamber will have to weigh the words and the -- the hearsay evidence of this witness on what happened with all the other evidence, and that's what we'll do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you testified at page 17978 that the Skorpions unit: "They belonged to the Slavonia Baranja corps, I think the 11th, but they were also answerable to the detached Ministry of Defence headquartered in Erdut, headed by Milan Milovanovic," that's how the transcript read, "aka Mrgud. He was the boss or the chief because he was the assistant minister of defence and had, by virtue of I know which authority, boundless, limitless powers." Now I believe that what you said was, "by virtue of I don't know which authority," if that is in fact the case, what did you mean when you said that? Who was it that gave Mrgud that boundless, limitless authority. Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either Martic, that's to say President Martic, or the minister of the Army of the Krajina, Colonel Suput. Nobody else. Of course, let me just correct you. Milanovic, whatever person he may have been, didn't have any card [as interpreted]. I don't know where you got that information from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there must be some sort of confusion because on page 82, line 6, there's a card. But that's not what the witness said. He said something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said Milanovic, whatever person he may have been, didn't have any ... What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A guard of sorts. A guard would be an elite unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this -- there's another confusion. On page 82, lines between 18 and 23, again, there is confusion there as well with what is on transcript. But I refrained from intervening because of time constraints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's serious you should do. If you consider it not of such importance that you refrain, we'll follow that. Ms. Marcus, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now earlier, Mr. Djukic, you acknowledged that you were not aware of the relationship between Milanovic and the Serbian DB. You said you were aware of his relationship with the public security and Badza, but you acknowledged that for that individual and a number of others you were not aware of their relationship, if any, to the Serbian DB. That's accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was on a close terms with Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Vlastimir Djordjevic, Rodja, both as a friend and in professional terms. The letter being here now with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 17979 you were asked: "Mr. Djukic, you said that they were part" -- this is referring to the Skorpions. "You said that they were part of the Slavonia Baranja Corps. Do you know who members of this battalion the Skorpions received their orders from?" You answered: "On certain issues from General Loncar, or the officer authorised by him. On the issue of providing security for the oil plant, from the director of the oil company. And on some other specific issues, from Milanovic." Now, the knowledge you have regarding who was giving orders to the Skorpions dates from which years, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well they were formed sometime in 1992, and I said that they had a dual role that was to maintain positions and to provide technical support to the oil plant which was very vulnerable because of possible sabotage. Now, as for the relationship between Loncar and Milanovic, that's not something I can speak to. I think, and a confirmation of this I got yesterday, that they were well co-ordinated and harmonised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, why not answer the question, Mr. Djukic? The question was: What years. You had your knowledge. Ms. Marcus asks the dates from which years. You started to say that they were formed sometime in 1992. That is about years. And it went up to when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what else am I supposed to answer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you gave knowledge regarding who was given orders to the Skorpions. You had mentioned two sources: Providing security for the oil plant; and, on other specific issues, Milanovic. Now, the only thing Ms. Marcus is asking you is receiving instructions from two sides. That was during what period of time. That was the question. And perhaps I could assist you. You said they were formed in 1992. Does that mean that receiving orders both from -- to say the oil plant side and from Milanovic on specific issues, that started right once the formation -- once the unit had been formated -- formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Save for Milanovic who had continuity; whereas, the corps commander and the directors changed between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now this situation of receiving instructions or orders from both directions, that continued until when? Until 1995 or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the way through to the point when the Skorpions left the districts in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they left the district. And then I met Mr. Milanovic -- well, you did ask me to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you're invited to answer the question. The question -- the answer is: This went on from 1992 to 1996. That's an answer to the question. So do not start explaining an answer that has not yet been given. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, even within those years, you were not aware of every instruction or every order that was given to Milanovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the military component is concerned, I wasn't aware of a single order. I've already said repeatedly that I didn't have any co-operation or was on good terms with the RSK army because I predicted their imminent breakup or demise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll take that as a yes answer. So you were not aware of every instruction or every order given to Milanovic; yes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then you were also not aware of all the details of every instruction or every order given to or received by the Skorpions; is that correct? Yes or no, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At page 17991, as you were starting to tell us about your investigation into the NIK oil company at Dzeletovci, you were asked: "Can you now tell us, please, did you know or did you inform the military authorities about the activities that you intended to undertake at the NIK?" Your answer was: "Your Honours, if I may just clarify something. Even had the Defence asked me --" and then you were cut off. Can you specify for us what you were going to say? Even had the Defence asked you, do you remember what you were going to say. If you don't remember, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. They were all stressful situations. This is my answer. This was a criminal inquiry into the crimes and their perpetrators, and this was something that I was not duty-bound to inform the Army of at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now you testified that you were assigned to investigate the operations of the oil industry. I believe you told us that this was in January and February of 1994. You said: "Two inspectors arriving from Knin, they are economists, and they were able to inspect the financial dealings of the company; whereas, I was only there in order to assist them in drafting a report and possibly a criminal complaint, if that was required." Who was it who assigned you to investigate the operations of the oil industry? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a continuous activity. I said that President Martic obtained the information. Krsto Zarkovic and I planned the action, IKOR [phoen] and that was part of it. As chief of public security, I didn't have anyone to receive information from when it comes to operative information. It is my duty to give a -- posit orders to others and get involved in matters if they deserve my attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps just to clarify, under whose authority was the investigation conducted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation was conducted, pursuant to the Law on Criminal Proceedings which authorises official persons when there are grounded suspicions that a crime would be committed, they would then be activated automatically. So there is no order. There is no need for an order to be issued. You just had to take action pursuant to law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what specifically were the allegations that were being investigated? Please, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In brief, President Martic noticed that the proceeds in -- into the budget were diminished, and he was wondering whether there was an illegal outflow of capital from the oil industry. And it was established that that was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was the outflow going to? So whether there was an illegal outflow of capital, to whom did you discover that it was being transferred to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discovered, and I already replied, there was a road under construction, some 35 kilometres of road through the region. It was 7 metres wide. The work was done by a private company, Borovica from Ruma, and the investigation established that there was less asphalt and gravel used for the road, and this involved a huge amount of money, and then Borovica from this money that was channeled out, syphoned out, he gave it to Egic who was then a member of the assembly. He gave it to them. And he is today one of the richest men in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now who did you send the reports to once the investigation was concluded? Please, Mr. Djukic, try to answer very briefly. I'm trying to ask you some questions so that we can follow up on this afterwards. And my time is very short. I'm nearly done. Please, very briefly, to whom did you send the final reports of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criminal complaint against the two individuals was forwarded to the competent district public prosecutor, Petar Stupar, who was a very honourable and very conscientious man, very conscientious worker. And this was a crime that involved immediate detention; in other words, the detention of these individuals would follow immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were there any police officials involved in the investigation apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, just wondering what the relevance is of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's hard to answer, Your Honour, without -- this is the first time we heard of it. I just want this answer to this one question, and then we'll determine what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It was led by the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So for us, when something is led, it wasn't in the notice, and we don't know. There obviously must have been some relevance because they raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That was my final question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, were there any other police officials with you involved in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, other than Kostic, Kojic, and the minister, there are no other officials. All the other persons were professionals, workers. They were police officers, commanders, chiefs. Krsto Radovic [as interpreted], for instance, is a -- has a Ph.D. now and is an instructor or a lecturer in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information. Do you say that many other persons were involved, therefore, in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was precise. Two inspectors who specialised in -- in white-collar crime, Krsto Zarkovic and me, the four of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the Skorpions and you spoke about Slobodan Medic, this at is 17992, you spoke about Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza, being a frequent guest of Medic. And you mentioned that Milovan Terzic also visited, if I understood you correctly? Can you tell who Milovan Terzic was? Please, very briefly sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovan Terzic was one of the managers of the oil industry, but he did not live in Serbia. He lived in Mirkovci. And for some reason that was not known to me, he spent a lot of time with the leadership of the public security in Serbia, and he was even given gifts by them. He received some resolvers from them. Now why it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, apparently Mr. Petrovic has nothing to bring to our attention at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, because in the meantime what I thought was omitted from the transcript was actually there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the court officer please call up P1061.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unnecessary to remind you that you've got five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see before you is a military report on paramilitary units. We say that this document dates from after May 1996. Your Honours I refer you to the transcript at the 27th of October, 2010, at page 8206. I'll give you a minute to just read through the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Would my colleague please tell me who the author of this document is? And where it's from, what organ, so that the witness may get his bearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is invited to read this document. If you would have presented it to him you would have given him perhaps other information. We do not know yet what the questions are, so it's premature to say that for the questions to follow that you would need to give this information to the witness, Mr. Petrovic. The witness may read the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I specifically ask you to read from where number 1 starts, that paragraph, and then the paragraph which will be on your next page.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down the second page. It has to be scrolled down a bit. Could you lift up the first page. The Serbian version. I don't see the bottom of it. I didn't see the bottom. Yes, now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have two very brief questions on this. Were aware of the Skorpions' involvement in the smuggling of lumber? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did your investigation involve that issue in any way? Yes or no, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A large quantity of lumber was seized, and, you know, not to mention that the judges sold it after I left from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, did your investigation also involve shipments of oil to Serbia, other than the -- the transfer of moneys. You told us earlier that your investigation involved the transfer of money. Now you told us it also involved the smuggling of lumber. Did your investigation also involve shipments of oil to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oil did not go to Serbia. The crude oil was sent to Serbia and then it was refined and processed in Pancevo. But I'm no expert for that, so I couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, your investigation did not involve the transfer or the shipment of crude oil to Serbia from Dzeletovci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We just had information as to the quantities that had gone there and we did that. However, the technology or the way they worked was such that they could always deceive you as to the quantities and the amounts that actually were exported out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, have I two questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I earlier told you several times that you could be more efficient by not going through all these documents. We have to stop not later than quarter past 2.00. I have a commitment outdoors. I told you that you would have time until quarter to 2.00. Therefore, I will now give an opportunity to Mr. Jordash. If the last final ten minutes leave some time, we will consider whether to grant that time to you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Jordash:

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Returning to the subject, if I may, of Kojic and his links with the DB. You said today at transcript 63, in relation to the fact that you did not know he had links with the DB, that he most certainly would not have told us about it, or anyone else, because that would have caused a lot of discontent among us. You also said at page 73 today that Prijic had effectively accused Kostic of having links to the DB at a meeting where Prijic was complaining about being kidnapped by Kostic. Was an association with the DB at that time within your region considered to be an insult?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the contrary. Why would it be considered to be insult? Why would it be wrong to be a collaborator with your own state, with your own country? Every Englishman who travels abroad actually notes down information that might be useful for his service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me qualify that, then. So it was considered to be okay to be an operative collecting intelligence for the Serbian DB; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not being an operative. But if we learned some information that would of interest to Serbia, it would be quite logical that that may pose a threat to us as well and that as such we should send them the information. But we did have telegram communication with the public security station -- sector of Serbia about crime and law and order and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why did you say that Kojic wouldn't have told you about his links with the DB because it would have caused discontent? Why -- why would that have been?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, discontent, that's something else, and I was precise. But you want me to answer briefly. You have to know what it is that the security service does. A collaborator is a person who -- in an organised manner and permanently provides information. He works under a code-name, and he is not allowed to disclose that information. As for discontent, that was a reference exclusively to our pay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. So in any event, Kojic you -- he never asserted any relationship with the DB, and you never worked out he had any relationship with the DB. Did you know if he had a relationship with the public security of Serbia in the time you worked with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I, too, was in direct contact with General Milic who was the chief of the crime prevention service. We co-ordinated our work. We worked together on a smuggling of vehicles and tobacco and so on, and I don't see anything wrong on that. To this day we co-operate along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash we are close to the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I know. But other issues arose during the Prosecution's examination. I was hoping to get about ten, even that would be too short, but -- it's difficult to cover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you have dealt with now arose before that, I think. But I'm not quite sure, so I have to be careful there. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we will be able to complete our re-examination by 2.15. I will try to be shorter than I originally thought I would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much minutes would you need, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may retain the 15 minutes that I announced originally when you first asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five more minutes for you, Mr. Jordash, at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just answer the question simply without any extra detail. Please help me. Did Kojic tell you or others, or did you become aware that he was linked with the public security in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that he never told me that he had any legal status there, employment. But we did talk, and there was communication. We had meetings with Republika Srpska also because crime was on the rise at the time, and co-operation is normal in police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just coming to your comment about Kojic being number two to Martic. Was Martic responsibile for the RSK army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces of Krajina under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm interested in how you place Kojic at number two, given what -- the evidence that you've given us; i.e., that he was arrested by elements of the RSK army, that he had no command authority over Arkan and that group, and that he was dealing with police issues in the main. Why do you say number two? Are you talking formally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you came by that information that Kojic had been arrested. There are a lot of errors in the interpretation, and I have never reacted because I was interrupted enough as it were. I never said anything about Kojic having ever been arrested. And another matter, Kojic was in charge of the police, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Right. So Kojic wasn't in charge of anything else other than the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly. And also of co-ordination with other structures. I don't know if you understand what co-ordination is, if that comes across clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So the co-ordination between the police and other structures, he was in charge of that, too?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And that was limited to SBWS; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you meant by the acronym. We don't have that acronym in our language. Do you mean the Slavonia Baranja region? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You even stayed within your next five minutes. You would have had one minute left. Mr. Petrovic, if you would perform similarly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do believe I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djukic, a couple of questions only to clarify certain issues, and please be brief. At the time of the takeover of Samac - that's to say the 16th and the 17th of April in 1992 - how many people were there in the 17th Tactical Group? What was their head count roughly or precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic -- One second. One second, please. Mr. Petrovic, a similar performance is not achieved by speaking at double speech. Could you read the transcript to see if the whole of your question was translated and transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put the question this way, Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as you do it slowly, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, how many men were there in the 4th battalion in Samac in mid-April 1992? How many members were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely 550 and another 150 would have been needed to have the full complement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many members did the 1st Battalion number? The one in Obudovac and Batkusa in the month of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six hundred. That was the best battalion, and later became an elite unit when it was taken over by the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many members did the 2nd and 3rd Battalions have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Between 500 and 600. Not all of them were active duty at all times. Some of them would reside in their homes. They were farmers and would be called when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the volunteers who arrived Batkusa by helicopter. How many of them were, roughly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with full responsibility less than 30, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
